title: Adaptive batch timeout exploration (scratchpad)
content:
Context / goal:
- Quick exploration of adaptive batch-timeout (coalescing window) as a knob to trade p50/p95 latency vs tokens/sec and overall cost.
- Hypothesis: short fixed timeout (2-5ms) is good for low-latency small-seq requests but wastes throughput for mixed/long-seq workloads; dynamic timeout based on recent sequence-length distribution and utilization can improve cost while keeping tail latency acceptable.

Test harness and dataset:
- Model: redwood-7b-quant (fp16->int8 quant profile) on single A100-80GB.
- Runner: benchmonkey v0.4 (simple client generating async requests, exposes qps, lat quantiles).
- Workload: 10k-sample production-like trace (copied anonymized) with: 65% short <64 tokens, 25% mid 64-512 tokens, 10% long >512 tokens. Requests per-second targeted: 200 qps steady; spike tests up to 600 qps.
- Configs: batch_timeout_ms ∈ {2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, adaptive}. Adaptive policy implemented in benchmonkey shim: observes last 1s of request lengths and utilization and sets timeout = clamp( base_ms * (1 + avg_len/256), min=2, max=80 ) where base_ms tuned to hit desired utilization.

Commands used (local):
- warmup: benchmonkey --trace trace.json --qps 200 --warmup 120 --model redwood-7b-quant --device 0
- run: benchmonkey --trace trace.json --qps 200 --duration 600 --model redwood-7b-quant --device 0 --batch-timeout-ms 10
- adaptive run: benchmonkey --adaptive-batching --trace trace.json --qps 200 --duration 600 --model redwood-7b-quant --device 0

Raw aggregated results (each row is mean over 3 runs, same cluster config):
- batch_timeout=2ms: qps achieved 198, avg latency 34ms, p50 28ms, p95 110ms, p99 410ms, tokens/sec 520k, notes: many small batches -> low p50 but p99 very high on long tails, GPU utilization 37%.
- batch_timeout=5ms: qps 198, avg 38ms, p50 33ms, p95 95ms, p99 280ms, tokens/sec 580k, GPU util 44%.
- batch_timeout=10ms: qps 200, avg 52ms, p50 45ms, p95 120ms, p99 240ms, tokens/sec 720k, GPU util 61%.
- batch_timeout=20ms: qps 200, avg 78ms, p50 65ms, p95 150ms, p99 280ms, tokens/sec 860k, GPU util 75%.
- batch_timeout=50ms: qps 200, avg 160ms, p50 140ms, p95 260ms, p99 540ms, tokens/sec 1.02M, GPU util 88%.
- batch_timeout=100ms: qps 200, avg 310ms, p50 280ms, p95 520ms, p99 900ms, tokens/sec 1.06M, GPU util 91%.
- adaptive policy: qps 200, avg 60ms, p50 50ms, p95 130ms, p99 260ms, tokens/sec 825k, GPU util 68%.

Notes on behavior observed:
- Very low timeouts (2-5ms) prioritize latency for short requests but starve throughput: long-seq requests end up in few huge batches causing p99 spikes.
- Large timeouts boost tokens/sec but increase p50/p95 for the common short requests a lot. 50-100ms delays are unbearable for interactive use.
- Adaptive policy delivered the best balance: tokens/sec close to 10ms-20ms fixed settings but p50 substantially lower than those fixed settings. p99 sits between 10ms and 20ms fixed runs.
- GPU util correlates with tokens/sec but not linearly with latency; batching helps utilization but introduces queuing latency that affects short requests disproportionately.

Micro-observations (from sampling request logs):
- During adaptive runs, timeout oscillated between 6-18ms aligned with bursts of long sequences.
- When bursts of long seqs occur, adaptive raised timeout and absorbed long sequences into larger batches, smoothing the p99 spike.
- Cold-start/warmup still problematic: first 30s of a run have lower GPU util and higher p99 across configs; need separate warmup policy.

Cost-ish back-of-envelope:
- baseline cost estimate per 1M tokens (serverized pricing approximated):
  - batch_timeout 5ms => token throughput 580k => ~1.72 \"+units\" per 1M tokens (placeholder metric).
  - adaptive => token throughput 825k => ~1.21 units per 1M tokens.
(Interpretation: adaptive saves ~30% on token-cost for same QPS profile.)

Quick conclusions / recommendations:
1) Adaptive batch timeout works for mixed-length workloads; it reliably improved tokens/sec and lowered p50 compared to aggressive fixed timeouts while keeping p99 similar to moderate fixed timeouts.
2) For interactive public API we probably want a hybrid: short fixed cap (e.g., 5ms) for premium low-latency routes + adaptive batching for default routes.
3) Add warmup-specific policy: for newly spun-up model worker, use conservative shorter timeout until GPU utilization stabilizes (to avoid initial large p99s).
4) Improve adaptive policy heuristics: include in-flight batch size, time-since-last-served and explicit burst-detection (detect sudden uptick in long-seq fraction) to damp oscillation.
5) Need A/B against smart-routing fallback: compare adaptive batching + routing long requests to dedicated long-seq pool vs adaptive-only.

Next steps (actionable):
- [ ] Run 24h continuous test with production trace to measure steady-state drift and long-tail rare events (weekend/overnight patterns).
- [ ] Add telemetry for adaptive decisions (hist of timeouts per second, reasons) and push to console dashboard.
- [ ] Prototype warmup policy and re-run 3x baseline to measure p99 improvement.
- [ ] Share results w/ serving-runtime and product (Lena / Elliot) to propose API-level routing knob for long-seq heavy routes.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How stable is adaptive when multiple workers with different histories compete behind load balancer? (might need global coordinator or sticky routing)
- Cost metric requires proper calibration vs infra pricing; above numbers are relative and need to map to $/token properly.
- Impact when combined with prefix caching: if many requests hit KV cache, effective sequence length distribution changes — adaptivity should consider cache-hit adjusted length.

Scratchpad logs / useful snippets:
- example log line (benchmonkey):
  [2026-03-10 10:14:32] qps=200 act_qps=199 batch_timeout=12ms batches/s=330 avg_batch_size=5 gpu_util=69 p50=49ms p95=128ms p99=258ms

- quick plot notes (to reproduce):
  - x-axis: batch_timeout (ms) or adaptive; y-left: tokens/sec (bar); y-right: p99 (line). Expected to show tokens/sec rising with timeout, p99 U-shaped (low at tiny timeout? actually high for tiny due to big long-batch spikes).

Bottom line: adaptive batch timeout is promising; it consistently improved throughput while keeping interactive latency for the common short requests near acceptable. Need longer run experiments + integration with warmup and routing to validate for production rollout.

Notes-to-self: save benchmonkey config and raw traces under personal drive folder ~/bench/ with tags experiment-2026-03-adaptive. Archive run artifacts to S3: s3://redwood-inference-experiments/adaptive-batch/2026-03-10/
